steps.title: The whole machine, then zoom in
steps.text:
OVERVIEW · STEP 1 OF 20
The whole machine, then zoom in

An LLM does one thing: given the tokens so far, score every possible next token. This lesson covers the first three boxes.

WHAT IT IS

A large language model (LLM) is one function: in goes the text so far, out comes a score for every token in its vocabulary. The boxes: a tokenizer (text → token IDs), an embedding table (each ID → a list of numbers, plus its position), attention (each token pulls in context from earlier tokens), an MLP (multi-layer perceptron: a small network applied to each token on its own), with attention + MLP stacked N times (one attention + MLP pair is a layer), then scores over the whole vocabulary: one number per token, higher means likelier to come next.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
An assembly line: raw material enters, each station reshapes it, one product (the next word) comes out. Then the line runs again with that word added to the input.
Technical
A request pipeline: parse → look up → join with context → transform → rank every candidate → return one. Called in a loop, each response appended to the next request.
× N layers (32 in an 8B model)

token

Lesson 2: MLP, layers, picking a token
Run ▶

Press Run to send “The river bank” through. The orange chip shows what travels between boxes.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Llama 3 8B, for example, has a 128,000-token vocabulary, vectors 4,096 numbers wide, and 32 layers of attention + MLP. A 100-token answer means about 100 passes through the machine, one per new token.

EVIDENCE

Layer count, width and vocabulary size for Llama 3 8B, 70B and 405B are listed in Table 3 of the Llama 3 paper. Llama Team, The Llama 3 Herd of Models (2024) ↗

Go deeper

The output is a score for every token in the vocabulary, not a sentence. To write a sentence, the model picks one likely token, appends it to the input, and runs the whole machine again: one full pass per new token. Attention and MLP alternate, and that pair repeats N times (32 layers in Llama 3 8B). Backend version: a stateless function called in a loop, each response appended to the next request.

steps.title: Models read numbers, not text
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.1 · STEP 2 OF 20
Models read numbers, not text

A tokenizer cuts text into pieces from a fixed list (the vocabulary) and swaps each piece for its ID. Type anything.

WHAT IT IS

A tokenizer splits text into tokens (pieces from a fixed list called the vocabulary) and replaces each with its token ID, a number. The model only ever sees these numbers.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A library catalogue: books are found by call number, not by reading every cover. The number stands for the book.
Technical
A lexer turning source code into tokens before the parser runs, combined with a dictionary encoder (like Huffman or gzip) that maps frequent pieces to codes.
The
42316
river
48633
bank
33535
flood
2445
ed
41780

The small number under each piece is its token ID.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Modern tokenizers use byte-pair encoding (BPE): start from single bytes, then repeatedly merge the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size (roughly 50k–200k). Training the tokenizer happens once, before the model is trained, and then it's frozen.

EVIDENCE

Subword units let a model with a fixed vocabulary handle any word, including rare and unknown ones, by spelling them from smaller pieces. Sennrich et al., Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (2015) ↗

Go deeper

The small number under each piece is its ID. Try unbelievable or flooooded: a word the tokenizer has never seen still works, because it splits into pieces it knows. This is a toy tokenizer with a tiny vocabulary; real ones have 50k to 200k pieces. Real tokenizers also keep case and the leading space: ' bank', 'bank' and 'Bank' are different tokens with different IDs.

steps.title: Choose the size of the pieces
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.1 · STEP 3 OF 20
Choose the size of the pieces

Small pieces make long sequences; big pieces need a huge vocabulary. Subwords (pieces between a letter and a word) sit in between.

WHAT IT IS

The piece size is a trade-off between sequence length (how many tokens a text becomes) and vocabulary size (how many distinct pieces the model must know).

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Packing for a move: tiny boxes mean hundreds of trips; one giant box per room is impossible to lift. Medium boxes win.
Technical
Choosing a page or chunk size: too small and per-item overhead dominates; too large and you waste space on things you rarely need.
Characters
Subwords

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Characters make sequences long, and attention cost grows with the square of length. Whole words need millions of entries and fail on any unseen word. Subwords keep both reasonable and can still spell any text.

Go deeper

Characters: the sequence gets long, and attention compares every token with every earlier one, so cost grows with the square of length (you'll see this near the end of 1.4). Words: a word not in the list becomes [UNKNOWN] and the model learns nothing about it, and rare words barely get trained. Subwords: any text can be built from known pieces.

steps.title: The model never sees letters
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.1 · STEP 4 OF 20
The model never sees letters

The model sees token IDs, not letters, so it can't reliably count the r's in “strawberry”. Switch to what it actually receives.

WHAT IT IS

Each token is one opaque ID. “strawberry” arrives as a few IDs like str + aw + berry; the letters inside each piece are not part of the input.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Counting the letters in someone's name when you only have their employee number.
Technical
Being asked to count characters in a string when the service only receives customer_id = 48213: the information isn't in the request.
Pieces
What the model sees
str
aw
berry

What you see: three pieces, letters visible.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

To count the r's, the model would have to have memorized how each token is spelled and add across pieces. The same cause breaks reversing words, rhyming, and arithmetic on long numbers.

EVIDENCE

Andrej Karpathy traces many odd LLM behaviours, spelling and arithmetic among them, back to tokenization. Let's build the GPT Tokenizer ↗

Go deeper

To count letters the model would have to have memorized how each of its token IDs is spelled. Same root cause for reversing words, rhymes and long-number arithmetic. Backend version: counting the characters in a customer's name when you only receive customer_id.

steps.title: Other languages pay more
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.1 · STEP 5 OF 20
Other languages pay more

In this toy, the same sentence costs 4 tokens in English and 36 in Hindi, because it has no Hindi pieces at all. Real tokenizers do better, but other languages still cost more.

WHAT IT IS

A tokenizer learns its pieces from its training text. Languages it saw less of get fewer merged pieces, so the same meaning takes more tokens, down to raw bytes in the worst case.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A phrasebook written for English speakers: common English phrases are one entry; anything else must be spelled out letter by letter.
Technical
A compression dictionary trained on English logs, then applied to other data: it still works, but it barely compresses.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

More tokens means higher cost (billed per token), slower generation (one token per step), less room in the context window, and usually lower quality. Training the model later can't fix it, because the tokenizer is frozen first.

EVIDENCE

The same text translated into different languages can differ in token count by up to 15×, even with tokenizers built for multilingual use, which affects cost, latency, and how much fits in context. Petrov et al., Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages (2023) ↗

Go deeper

More tokens for the same meaning means higher cost (billed per token), slower output (one token per step), less fits in the context window, and usually worse quality. Training the model afterwards can't fix it, because the tokenizer was built and frozen first. Real tokenizers have some Hindi pieces, so the gap is smaller than this toy's, but it's real. Backend version: a compression dictionary trained on English logs, used on other data.

steps.title: A vector is just a list of numbers
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.2 · STEP 6 OF 20
A vector is just a list of numbers

A vector is a list of numbers; two numbers draw as an arrow (how far right, how far up). Embeddings are vectors. Move the sliders.

WHAT IT IS

A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Two numbers can be drawn as an arrow (right, up); models use lists of thousands, which can't be drawn but follow the same rules.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
GPS coordinates: two numbers pin a place on a map. Change one and the place moves.
Technical
A fixed-length feature array, float[4096], like a row of numeric columns in a table.
first number (money-ness): 2
second number (water-ness): 1
[2, 1]
money-ness →
water-ness ↑
v

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

In a model, every token becomes a vector of a few thousand numbers. No single number means much; the meaning is in where the whole vector points.

Go deeper

Real embeddings have thousands of numbers, so you can't draw them, but every rule that follows works the same way with 2 numbers or 4,096. The names money-ness and water-ness are labels for this toy only.

steps.title: Each ID picks a row
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.2 · STEP 7 OF 20
Each ID picks a row

The embedding table has one row of numbers per token. “Embedding a token” just means reading its row. Tap a word.

WHAT IT IS

The embedding table has one row (a vector) per token in the vocabulary. Embedding a token means looking up its row by ID.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A dictionary where each word's entry is a list of numbers instead of a definition.
Technical
Map<tokenId, float[]>, or a categorical feature lookup: you'd never do arithmetic on a user ID, so you map each ID to learned numbers.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

100,000 rows × 4,096 numbers ≈ 410 million learned numbers, just for this table. The same token always reads the same row; context is added later, by attention.

Go deeper

Rows = vocabulary size (set by the tokenizer). Row width = a design choice, like 768 in a small model or 4,096 in a mid-size 7–8B model; the largest use about 16–18k. 100,000 × 4,096 is about 410 million numbers. bank reads the same row in “The river bank flooded” and “I deposited cash at the bank”: the table has no idea of context. Its first two numbers sit halfway, [0.50, 0.50]. Why not feed the ID itself? IDs are labels, not quantities. 1001 and 1002 are unrelated, like auto-increment keys, so arithmetic on them is meaningless.

steps.title: Training moves similar words together
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.2 · STEP 8 OF 20
Training moves similar words together

Training pulls words used in similar sentences close together. Rows start random; every correction nudges them. Drag the slider and watch bank land between water and money.

WHAT IT IS

Rows start as random numbers. During training the model keeps predicting the next word, and every mistake nudges the rows involved. Words used in similar sentences get similar nudges.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
People who keep turning up at the same events end up in the same friend group, without anyone assigning them.
Technical
Collaborative filtering: users who buy similar things end up with similar learned vectors, with no one labelling them.
training progress: 0%
cash
deposit
loan
river
stream
lake
bank

Each dot is one word's row, drawn in 2D. Left/right and up/down mean nothing on their own; only the distance between dots matters. Near the end of training the groups take colours: teal = money words, blue = water words, black = bank.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

“The ___ overflowed” and “fish swim in the ___” push river and stream in the same directions, so their rows drift together over billions of examples. Nobody labels them as water; their usage does. bank is used in both water and money sentences, so it ends up between the two clusters.

EVIDENCE

The word2vec models learned high-quality word vectors from 1.6 billion words in under a day, and the vectors captured both syntactic and semantic similarity. Mikolov et al., Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (2013) ↗

Go deeper

A 2D picture of what really happens in thousands of dimensions. Nobody labels “river” as water: sentences like “the ___ overflowed” and “fish swim in the ___” push river and stream the same way. bank appears in both water and money sentences, so it settles between them. Backend version: recommendation systems learn user and item vectors the same way, and similar behaviour ends up nearby.

steps.title: Close means similar, and that is how it generalizes
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.2 · STEP 9 OF 20
Close means similar, and that is how it generalizes

Nearby rows give nearly the same output, so what the model learns about river carries over to stream. Tap two words to measure their distance.

WHAT IT IS

The distance between two rows is computable. Generalization means applying what was learned from one example to similar ones the model never saw.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Having learned to drive one car, you can drive a similar one, because the controls are close to what you know.
Technical
Nearest-neighbour search: similar inputs land near each other, so a decision made for one point transfers to its neighbours.
cash
deposit
loan
river
stream
lake
bank

river ↔ stream: distance 1.7 (close: the model treats them alike)

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Everything after the embedding is built from smooth functions (multiply, add, softmax, gentle curves), so small input changes give small output changes. What the model learns from “the river flooded” carries over to “the stream flooded”. Models usually measure the angle between vectors (cosine similarity).

Go deeper

Everything after the embedding is built from smooth functions (multiply, add, softmax, gentle curves), so small input changes give small output changes. That means what the model learns from “the river flooded” carries over to “the stream flooded”. bank sits between the clusters; 1.4 shows how its sentence pulls it to one side. That is generalization. Real models usually measure the angle between vectors (cosine similarity) rather than straight distance; the idea is the same.

steps.title: Position: order changes meaning
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.2 · STEP 10 OF 20
Position: order changes meaning

Embeddings say what a token is, not where. Without position, “river bank” and “bank river” give bank the identical vector. Turn position on: a learned slot vector is added, so order changes the sum.

WHAT IT IS

Position information tells the model where each token is. Attention by itself compares contents, not places, so without it, reordering the words hands attention the same vectors.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Pages of a letter with no page numbers dropped on the floor: all the words are there, the meaning isn't.
Technical
TCP sequence numbers: packets can arrive in any order; the numbers let the receiver rebuild the stream.
Without position
With position
river bank
bank river
river
slot 0
bank
slot 1
bank

bank [0.5, 0.5] + nothing = [0.5, 0.5] in both orders

Flip the order: nothing changes. Attention compares contents, not places, so it can't tell “river bank” from “bank river” (apart from the weak hint in the panel below).

Blue = bank's content row; teal = its slot vector, added tip to tail (start it where bank ends); orange = the sum attention receives.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

The original Transformer adds a position vector to each token's row, as in the visual; a learned version is a second table with one row per slot (a hard length limit). Most modern models use RoPE (rotary position embedding) instead, which builds position into attention itself; it comes later in the course.

Nuance: models that only look backward can still pick up some sense of position on their own, from how many earlier tokens each one can see. Explicit position, usually RoPE, is still the standard design.

EVIDENCE

The original Transformer added position vectors to the token embeddings, and found learned position vectors and fixed formula-based ones gave nearly identical results. Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017), section 3.5 ↗

RoPE encodes absolute position as a rotation and builds relative distance into attention, with dependency that decays as tokens get farther apart. Su et al., RoFormer (2021) ↗

Language models that only look backward, trained with no positional encoding at all, still learned an implicit sense of absolute position and stayed competitive with standard models. Haviv et al., Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information (2022) ↗

Go deeper

Position also gives distance: a “river” right next to “bank” should count more than one 300 tokens back, and without position they're identical vectors. Older models add a second table with one row per slot, which is also a hard length limit. Most modern models use RoPE: a formula that rotates vectors by slot number, with no table. Backend version: TCP sequence numbers.

steps.title: Training writes. Using only reads.
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.2 · STEP 11 OF 20
Training writes. Using only reads.

Weights (the stored tables) never change when you use a model; activations (copies computed per request) are thrown away. Run some requests.

WHAT IT IS

Weights are the learned numbers (the embedding table and everything else); they change only during training. Activations are the vectors computed while handling one request; they're thrown away afterwards.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A recipe book versus tonight's cooking: you read the recipe, cook a meal, and the book is unchanged.
Technical
Read-only reference rows versus values computed in a SELECT: every request reads the table, none of them UPDATEs it.
embedding table read
weights · frozen
→ copy →
working vector
activation · temporary
→ later steps (1.3) →
discarded
after the request
Run a request

requests: 0 · rows written to the table: 0

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

At inference the weights are frozen, which is why one copy in GPU memory can serve many users at once. Each request's activations (its working vectors) are private and temporary.

Go deeper

Two kinds of numbers. Weights (the embedding table and every other learned number) change only during training. Activations are computed fresh for every request, then thrown away. RoPE works on the copy, never on the table. Backend version: weights are read-only database rows; activations are values computed in a SELECT, never an UPDATE.

steps.title: Dot product: how well two lists match
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.3 · STEP 12 OF 20
Dot product: how well two lists match

A dot product scores how well two lists match: multiply matching positions, then add. Same direction scores high, a right angle 0, opposite negative. Pick a B, or move it.

WHAT IT IS

The dot product multiplies two vectors position by position and adds the results into one number: large when they point the same way, zero at right angles, negative when opposite.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Matching a job's requirements against a candidate's skills: each skill counts only if both have it, and the total is the fit.
Technical
A weighted relevance score: sum(query[i] * doc[i]), the core of vector search.

A = bank's query [1, 1]: what bank is looking for. B = another word's key: what that word offers to match on. Both are made in 1.4; here, just the arithmetic. In “The river bank” the scores come out the 0, river 3, bank 2.

the's key [0, 0]
river's key [0, 3]
bank's key [1, 1]
cash's key [3, 0]
B first: 0
B second: 3

[1, 1] · [0, 3] = 1×0 + 1×3 = 3 (strong match)
angle θ = 45° · length of A = 1.41 · length of B = 3.00 · cosine = 0.71

A
river

The dot product grows with both alignment and length; divide by the lengths and you get cosine similarity, the angle-only version.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

It's the closeness idea from 1.2 as a single number. Attention uses it to score how relevant each earlier word is to the current one.

Go deeper

This is the closeness idea from 1.2 turned into one number. Attention uses it to answer “how relevant is that word to me?”

steps.title: Softmax: turn scores into percentages
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.3 · STEP 13 OF 20
Softmax: turn scores into percentages

Softmax turns any scores into positive shares that add up to 100%; bigger scores take a much bigger share. These are bank's scores from the dot product step: the 0, river 3, bank 2.

WHAT IT IS

Softmax turns any list of scores into positive shares that add up to 100%: raise e to each score, then divide each by the total.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Splitting a bonus pool by performance score: everyone gets a share, the best get much more, and the shares always add up to the pool.
Technical
Normalizing weights for weighted random selection, with an exponent that exaggerates the leader.
score for the: 0
score for river: 3
score for bank: 2
the
3.5%
river
70.5%
bank
25.9%

eˢᶜᵒʳᵉ: 1.0, 20.1, 7.4 → each ÷ 28.5 (their total)

Drag the scores to explore, then put them back to 0 / 3 / 2: the next step blends with 3.5% / 70.5% / 25.9%.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

The exponent keeps every share positive and stretches the gaps, so the top score wins clearly while the others keep a little. Shares must sum to 1 because the next step is an average.

EVIDENCE

3Blue1Brown animates softmax inside attention, including why it's the right choice for weights. Attention in transformers, step-by-step ↗

Go deeper

How: raise e (≈2.718) to each score, then divide each by the total. Raising to a power makes every share positive and stretches the gaps, so the winner wins clearly but losers keep a little. Why add up to 100%: the next step is an average, and an average needs shares that sum to 1.

steps.title: Weighted average: blend by the percentages
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.3 · STEP 14 OF 20
Weighted average: blend by the percentages

Mix vectors using the softmax shares as the recipe: 70.5% river, 25.9% bank, 3.5% the. Slide river's share and watch the blend move.

WHAT IT IS

A weighted average mixes several vectors, each multiplied by its share; the shares come from softmax.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Mixing paint: 70% blue and 30% yellow lands between the two, closer to blue.
Technical
A blended score in a ranking system: 0.7 × signalA + 0.3 × signalB.
river's share: 70.5% (bank gets the rest; the keeps 3.5%)

70.5% × river[0, 3] + 25.9% × bank[1, 1] + 3.5% × the[0, 0] = [0.26, 2.38]

money-ness →
water-ness ↑
river
bank
blend
Back to the softmax shares

At the softmax shares the blend is [0.26, 2.38]: mostly river, so it points toward water. You'll meet this exact vector again in 1.4.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Dot product (score every word) → softmax (scores to shares) → weighted average (blend) is all of attention. You'll see the three run together in 1.4.

Go deeper

Attention = dot product (score every word) → softmax (scores to percentages) → weighted average (blend). One more basic first: how training sets all these numbers.

steps.title: Gradient: how training nudges each number
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.3 · STEP 15 OF 20
Gradient: how training nudges each number

Training nudges each number in proportion to what it's multiplied by. To score “flooded” as the next word, bank's row meets flooded's output row [1, 3] (really via the layers, skipped here). Target 2; now −1.3. Press Train step.

WHAT IT IS

A gradient says, for each number, how much the error would change if that number moved a little. Training moves every number a small step in the direction that reduces the error.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Adjusting a recipe after tasting: too salty, so cut the salt most, because salt had the biggest effect on the taste.
Technical
A profiler for error: blame is attributed to each config value in proportion to how much it contributed, and each is adjusted accordingly, all at once.

score = bank's row · flooded's output row = 0.20×1 + (−0.50)×3 = -1.30

flooded's output row, first number (second fixed at 3); try 0: 1
bank's row (early in training)	value	multiplied by (flooded's output row)	last nudge
number 1	0.200	1	+0.000
number 2	-0.500	3	+0.000

-1.30

2.00

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Here the score for “flooded” is bank's row · flooded's output row: the model keeps a second learned table with one row per token, and a token's score as the next word is the dot product with its row. That's all this step needs; Lesson 2 shows where the table sits in the model. Backpropagation computes every number's gradient in one backward pass. Repeated over billions of sentences, these nudges set the embedding rows, the attention matrices, and everything else.

EVIDENCE

3Blue1Brown's chapters on gradient descent and backpropagation animate this. Gradient descent, how neural networks learn ↗

Go deeper

Where does flooded's output row come from? The model ends with a second learned table, one row per token, and scores each possible next token by a dot product with that row; Lesson 2 covers it. In a real model it's dotted with bank's final vector after all the layers, not the raw row; this toy skips the layers, and the nudge flows back through them to the row. Nudge = step size × how far off the score is × what the number is multiplied by. A number multiplied by 0 has no influence, so it never moves. Nobody picks a number: every number used in a prediction gets its own nudge, all calculated in one pass (backpropagation). Repeat over billions of sentences and the rows, every other learned table you'll meet in 1.4, everything, settle into useful values. That's all training is. Backend version: 4,096 config knobs, each adjusted in proportion to how sensitive the output is to it, measured all at once.

steps.title: bank has one row, but two meanings
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.4 · STEP 16 OF 20
bank has one row, but two meanings

Attention shifts bank's meaning to fit its sentence; its row never changes. Switch attention on, then change the sentence.

WHAT IT IS

Attention updates each word's vector using the words before it, so the same row ends up meaning different things in different sentences.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
“Bank” in a conversation: you work out which meaning from the words around it, not from the word alone.
Technical
Resolving a variable's value from its surrounding scope at runtime, rather than from its declaration alone.
Attention off
Attention on
The river bank flooded
I deposited cash at the bank
money
water
halfway
bank

Attention off: bank is just its row, [0.50, 0.50] in its first two numbers, halfway in both sentences.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

bank's row is the same in both sentences; the blended vector after attention is not. That blended vector is an activation, computed for this sentence and discarded after.

Go deeper

With attention off, bank is just its row: halfway between meanings, in both sentences. With it on, bank pulls in “river” or “cash” and moves. This is an activation: computed for this sentence, gone afterwards.

steps.title: The three basics, running together
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.4 · STEP 17 OF 20
The three basics, running together

Attention is the three basics in a row: score, softmax, blend. bank asks the same question (its query) in every sentence; each earlier word answers with its key. Step through, then switch the sentence.

WHAT IT IS

Each word computes a query (what it's looking for); every earlier word offers a key (what it matches on) and a value (what it hands over). Score = query · key, softmax, then blend the values.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Asking a room “who knows about water?”: people whose expertise matches answer loudest, and you take in a mix of what they say.
Technical
A search engine that returns a blend of every document, weighted by relevance, instead of only the top hit: a soft lookup.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

query = x × W_Q, key = x × W_K, value = x × W_V, where the three matrices are learned weights. Why three, and not the token's own vector for everything? Looking, matching and handing over are different jobs: what bank is looking for is not what makes it a good match for other words, nor what it should pass on. Separate learned matrices let each job be tuned on its own. Scores are divided by √(vector size) before softmax so they don't grow too large.

EVIDENCE

This is scaled dot-product attention as defined in the original transformer paper. Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017) ↗

Go deeper

Who decides the query? Nobody, by hand. query = bank's row × W_Q, where W_Q is a learned matrix shared by every token. Keys come from another learned matrix, W_K, and the vectors that get blended (values) from a third, W_V. Here values equal keys to keep it simple. All three matrices start random; wrong predictions nudge them until queries pull in useful context, the same way embedding rows learned in 1.2. The matrices are weights (frozen in use); each query, key and value is an activation. I picked [1, 1] so the arithmetic is easy; a real query has thousands of numbers nobody chose. Backend version: a search engine where every document comes back, blended by relevance, instead of only the top hit.

steps.title: Who does each token listen to?
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.4 · STEP 18 OF 20
Who does each token listen to?

Each token blends earlier tokens and itself. The number under each word is its share (arc thickness shows the same); “self” is the share a token keeps from its own vector. Tap any word, or switch sentences. Later words are greyed: a token only looks backward (why comes in 3.1).

WHAT IT IS

The attention weights (the softmax shares) say how much each word draws from each earlier word. They always add up to 1 per word.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Each person in a meeting deciding how much to weigh each earlier speaker.
Technical
A per-row weight vector over earlier rows, like a learned, content-based window function.
River sentence

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

A word only looks backward (the reason comes with training, in 3.1). Real models learn these weights; the ones shown are hand-picked to illustrate the pattern.

Go deeper

The weights for one token always add up to 1: it's a blend. Tap “flooded”: it leans on “bank” (what flooded?) and “river”. Weights here are hand-picked to show the idea; a real model learns them and spreads them over many heads and layers.

steps.title: Several heads: one blend per need
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.4 · STEP 19 OF 20
Several heads: one blend per need

A head is one copy of attention with its own softmax. One head's shares must add to 100%, so it can't focus sharply on two words at once. bank needs “river” (setting) and “the” (grammar). Compare.

WHAT IT IS

A head is one complete copy of attention with its own query, key and value matrices. Multi-head attention runs several heads side by side, joins their outputs, and multiplies by W_O, a learned square matrix that mixes the joined outputs (already the model's full width, e.g. 32 heads × 128 = 4,096) so the heads' findings can combine.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Asking several specialists the same question at once (a geographer, a grammarian) instead of one generalist who has to average their views.
Technical
Fanning one request out to several specialised indexes in parallel, then merging the responses.
One head
Two heads

45% river + 45% the + 10% bank = [0.50, 0.50, 0.50, 0.50]

Every output number is part river, part “the” (the mixed colour). The next layer only gets these four numbers: it can't tell which word contributed what. At 45 / 45 the two patterns cancel to a flat [0.50, 0.50, 0.50, 0.50]. Push river up and “the” must come down: one set of shares, adding to 100%.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Heads split the width rather than adding to it: 32 heads × 128 numbers = 4,096. Each head gets its own softmax, so it can focus sharply on its own target.

EVIDENCE

The original transformer introduced multi-head attention so the model can attend to information from different representation subspaces at once. Vaswani et al. (2017) ↗

Go deeper

A head is one complete copy of the attention calculation with its own W_Q, W_K, W_V. Heads run at the same time on the same words, independently. Heads split the width rather than adding to it: a model 4,096 wide with 32 heads gives each head 128 numbers, so 32 heads cost about the same as one wide head. Nobody assigns each head's question: they start from different random matrices and gradient nudges each toward whatever helps. The weights here are hand-picked to show the idea. Backend version: fan out one request to several specialized indexes in parallel, then merge the responses.

steps.title: Cost grows with the square of the context
steps.text:
CHAPTER 1.4 · STEP 20 OF 20
Cost grows with the square of the context

Every token scores every token it can see. Drag the slider: double the tokens, about four times the work.

WHAT IT IS

Every token scores itself and every earlier token: n(n+1)/2 scores for n tokens, about n²/2. So the number of scores grows with the square of the number of tokens.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Introductions at a party: with twice as many guests, there are about four times as many handshakes.
Technical
A self-join done as a nested loop: every row compared with itself and every earlier row.
tokens: 8
tokens it scores →
↓ token doing the looking

n(n+1)/2 = 36 scores for 8 tokens (each token scores itself and earlier ones)
136
scores for 16 tokens (×3.8, heading to ×4 as n grows)

≈ n²/2: doubling the context still ×4

At short context the per-token work (lookups, MLP) dominates; past tens of thousands of tokens the ≈ n²/2 scores take over.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

8,000 tokens → about 32 million scores; 16,000 → 128 million; 128,000 → about 8.2 billion, per head, per layer (≈ n²/2). This is why long context is expensive and why token counts matter.

EVIDENCE

Self-attention's time and memory grow quadratically with sequence length; FlashAttention speeds it up by reading and writing GPU memory more carefully, without approximating. Dao et al., FlashAttention (2022) ↗

Go deeper

Scores ≈ n²/2: 8,000 tokens → about 32 million; 16,000 → 128 million; 128,000 → about 8.2 billion, per head, per layer. Looking only backward is what halves n², and halving doesn't change how it scales: double the tokens, ×4 the scores. This is why long context is expensive and why token counts (step 5) matter. The rest of the model costs a fixed amount per token, so the square only wins at long context: Kaplan et al. found the context-dependent part stays a small fraction of compute while the model's width is more than the context length ÷ 12, which for a 4,096-wide model means up to about 49,000 tokens. Kaplan et al., Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (2020) ↗ Backend version: a self-join done as a nested loop.

The whole system map, then embeddings: the embedding matrix, directions that carry meaning, and the dot product.

Attention in transformers, step-by-step

Query, key, value, softmax and multiple heads, animated. It also covers the mask, which this course saves for 3.1.

THEN · LESSON STEP 15
Gradient descent, how neural networks learn
3Blue1Brown · Deep Learning Ch. 2

Training as rolling downhill on an error surface: every number moves in the direction that reduces the error.

THEN · LESSON STEP 15, GO DEEPER
Backpropagation, intuitively
3Blue1Brown · Deep Learning Ch. 3 · ~12–15 min

How each number's nudge is worked out: blame flows backward in proportion to influence.

OPTIONAL, LONG · LESSON STEPS 2–5
Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
Andrej Karpathy · ~2 h 13 min, hands-on code

Builds a real BPE tokenizer from scratch and traces odd LLM behaviour back to tokenization. Watch the opening for the why; the rest is code.

Go deeper

If Chapter 2 assumes too much, 3Blue1Brown's Chapter 1, “But what is a Neural Network?”, comes before it in the same series. These cover the same mechanisms as the lesson with different examples; seeing one idea two ways is what makes it stick.

steps.title: Check yourself
steps.text:
QUESTIONS
Check yourself

Answer each question out loud or in your notes before looking anything up. If one is hard, go back to its step.

1 · MECHANISM

Why do LLMs use subword tokens instead of characters or whole words? What breaks at each extreme?

2 · MECHANISM

Why can't an LLM reliably count the r's in “strawberry”?

3 · CONSEQUENCE

Why does the same paragraph cost more in Hindi than in English, and why can't training the model fix it?

4 · MECHANISM

Why can't a token ID be fed to the model as a plain number?

5 · MECHANISM

Nobody labels river and stream as related. How do their rows end up close, and why does that help the model?

6 · CONSEQUENCE

What breaks without position information? Give one example about order and one about distance.

7 · DISTINCTION

Which numbers change during training, which during use? How can RoPE work if use changes nothing?

8 · MECHANISM

Walk through one attention step for “bank”: query, keys, scores, weights, values, result.

9 · DESIGN

Why use three separate vectors (query, key, value) instead of the token's embedding for everything?

10 · MECHANISM

Who decides a token's query, and how does it get good at finding useful words?

11 · MECHANISM

What does softmax do to a list of scores, and why must the results add up to 100%?

12 · MECHANISM

During training, how does one column of an embedding row get changed? Why does one column move a lot while another doesn't move at all?

13 · DESIGN

Why do models run several attention heads instead of one, when the total width is the same?

14 · NUMBERS

Context goes from 8k to 16k tokens. What happens to attention's work, and which backend operation is this like?

15 · TRANSFER

A tokenizer has no piece for four spaces. What happens to cost and context when you send it Python code, and why?

16 · TRANSFER

Hallucination: how does “an LLM is a function, not a lookup table” explain it?

Then test yourself: ten scored questions with explanations and a list of what to study again. Take the quiz →
